What salt does to concrete

The chloride never stops arriving. A mix has to be designed for the shore it stands on.

5 min read

NJafrabad salt pans
On this page
  1. A bar in its bed
  2. How it arrives
  3. What happens at the bar
  4. Buying time
  5. The cheapest step
  6. What an owner can do
Field notes
  • Field notes overview

Essays

  • What salt does to concrete
  • The arithmetic of a cold kiln
  • Why we do not own three hundred machines
  • Basalt
  • Night shift in lion country
  • After the storm
  • How to read a shutdown
  • The first bus of the morning
  • The weighbridge

Reference

  • Glossary

Stand on a silo roof at Kovaya in the afternoon and lick your lips. You will taste the sea, though the shore is some way off. That taste is the subject of this note.

A bar in its bed

A reinforcing bar cast into good concrete is one of the safest pieces of steel on earth. Concrete is strongly alkaline, and in that alkaline bed the steel grows a skin, a film of oxide a few millionths of a millimetre thick, which stops it rusting. Engineers call the steel passive. It will sit there, bright as the day it was fixed, for a century.

Two things can take the skin away.

The first is slow and happens everywhere. Carbon dioxide from the air creeps into the concrete and, over decades, lowers its alkalinity from the surface inward. When that front reaches the steel, the skin is no longer stable.

The second is quicker, and it is the one that matters here. Chloride, the same ion that makes the sea salt, can break the skin even while the concrete is still fully alkaline. It does not need to wait for anything. It needs only to arrive at the bar in sufficient quantity.

How it arrives

On this coast it arrives on the wind. Breaking waves throw fine droplets into the air. The droplets dry to particles of salt, and the sea breeze carries them inland and sets them down on every surface. Then the dew comes, or the monsoon, and dissolves the salt, and the wet concrete drinks it in. The sun dries the surface and leaves the salt behind, a little deeper than before. The next night it happens again.

Wetting and drying, wetting and drying, three hundred and sixty-five times a year. Each cycle carries the chloride a little further. It travels through the pores that all concrete has, and it travels fastest through the pores of concrete that was made with too much water, compacted badly or cured for two days and forgotten.

What happens at the bar

When enough chloride has gathered at the steel, the skin fails at one point. A pit forms. Iron dissolves at the pit and reappears a little way off as rust.

Rust is a bulky thing. It takes up several times the room of the steel it came from. Inside hardened concrete there is no room. So the rust pushes, and concrete, which is strong when squeezed and weak when pulled apart, cracks.

The crack runs along the line of the bar to the surface. Now the salt has a road instead of a footpath. The corrosion quickens. A stain appears, the colour of tea. Then the cover comes away in a sheet, and the bar is in the open air, and what was a matter of chemistry has become a matter of structure.

From the first pit to the fallen cover can take a few years. From the day of casting to the first pit can take five years or fifty. The whole art lies in that second number.

Buying time

Nothing stops chloride. Everything we do is to slow it.

Depth. The further the bar lies from the surface, the longer the journey. That is what cover is for. The Indian code asks for 45 mm of it in a coastal environment and 50 mm where spray reaches, against 20 or 30 mm inland. The time chloride takes to reach the steel rises steeply with depth, so a bar fixed 20 mm too shallow has not lost a little of its protection. It has lost most of it. This is why we check cover blocks before every pour, and why an inspector who finds two missing has done the structure a favour.

Density. The fewer and finer the pores, the slower the journey. Pores come from surplus water, so the code limits the water in the mix more strictly on the coast. They come from air left in by poor compaction, so vibrators matter. And they come from concrete that dried before it had finished hardening, so curing matters, perhaps most of all.

Chemistry. Fly ash and slag, blended into the cement, do two useful things. They go on reacting for months and fill the pores with fresh solid. And they bind some of the chloride as it passes, taking it out of circulation. A blended-cement concrete, well cured, resists chloride far better than a plain one of the same strength. They are also slower to gain strength and less forgiving of neglect in the first week, which brings us back to curing.

Inhibitors and coatings. Admixtures that help the steel keep its skin a little longer. Coatings on the finished surface that keep the salt water out in the first place. Each buys years.

The cheapest step

Of all these, the one that costs least is water, kept on the concrete for the first ten days of its life. It is also the one most often skipped, because by then the pour is finished, the gang has moved on and nobody is watching.

We watch. The curing of every pour is recorded, and in May it is extended.

What an owner can do

If you own structures on this coast, three checks are worth more than any report.

Look for the tea-coloured stain, especially at corners and under ledges. Tap the surface with a small hammer and listen for the hollow note of concrete that has let go. And ask, of any new work, what the cover was and how long it was cured, and ask to see where that was written down.

A structure is not ruined by salt in a year. It is ruined in the first fortnight, by people who did not know what the air here carries, and the ruin takes twenty years to show.

The arithmetic of a cold kiln

Why minutes matter more than rates when a plant has stopped.

4 min read

NCement works, Kovaya
On this page
  1. The sum
  2. The second sum
  3. What the sums mean for a contractor
  4. A case
  5. Three things a plant can do
  6. And one thing a contractor must never do
Field notes
  • Field notes overview

Essays

  • What salt does to concrete
  • The arithmetic of a cold kiln
  • Why we do not own three hundred machines
  • Basalt
  • Night shift in lion country
  • After the storm
  • How to read a shutdown
  • The first bus of the morning
  • The weighbridge
  • One number

Reference

  • Glossary
  • Pocket checklists

Every plant manager knows this sum. Few contractors have been made to do it. We think it explains our whole business, so here it is.

The sum

Take a kiln that makes two hundred tonnes of clinker in an hour. That is not a large one by today’s standards.

It runs day and night. It does not rest on Sundays. In a good year it stops once, on purpose, for its annual repair.

Now something breaks. A gate jams, a duct tears, a foundation cracks under a fan. The kiln is stopped.

For every hour it stands, two hundred tonnes of clinker are not made. Not delayed. Not made. A kiln cannot run faster next week to catch up. It was already running as fast as it can. The hour is simply removed from the year.

Eight hours is sixteen hundred tonnes. A day is nearly five thousand.

Multiply by what a tonne is worth to you. We will not put a figure on it, because you know yours better than we do. Then set beside it the hourly rate of a crane, a welder and a rigger.

The two numbers are not of the same kind. One is written with a few digits. The other, with several more.

The second sum

There is worse. A kiln is not a light that can be switched off and on.

It is lined with brick, and brick that is heated or cooled too quickly cracks and falls. A kiln that has gone properly cold must be brought back to temperature over many hours, by a schedule the brick-makers lay down. Fuel is burned through all of those hours and no clinker is made.

So a stoppage long enough to let the kiln go cold costs the repair time, and then the heating time on top. A stoppage short enough to keep it hot costs only the repair. Between those two cases lies a cliff. On one side of it a breakdown is an expensive night. On the other it is an expensive week.

Which side a plant lands on is often decided in the first hour.

What the sums mean for a contractor

They mean that a plant with a kiln down is not buying fitting, welding or lifting. It is buying hours. Whoever can deliver the repair soonest is cheapest, almost regardless of the rate.

Suppose two contractors could do the same repair in the same six hours. One is thirty minutes from the gate. The other is five hours away. The second contractor would have to work for nothing, and then pay the plant a great deal, to be worth calling.

This is why we have never tried to be the cheapest firm on this coast by the hour. We have tried to be the nearest, the readiest and the one that needs no explaining to. On the plant’s side of the sum, those are the things that count.

A case

During a kiln breakdown at a major cement plant here, our civil and mechanical teams were on site within 25 minutes of the call. A contractor mobilising from outside the belt would have needed at least five hours. The plant resumed production eight hours ahead of its projected recovery.

Do the sum for those eight hours with your own kiln’s figure. That is what proximity is worth, once.

Three things a plant can do

The arithmetic also says something to the plant.

Agree the rates before the night. A negotiation at one in the morning is conducted in hours that cost two hundred tonnes each.

Open the gate in advance. Vendor registration, inductions and the names of supervisors lodged with security. Twenty minutes saved at the gate are twenty minutes of production.

Keep the number where the shift can see it. The engineer on nights should not have to wake someone to ask whom to call.

And one thing a contractor must never do

The sum tempts people to cut corners. If an hour is worth so much, surely the permit can wait, the gas test can be skipped, the man can go in without a harness just this once.

No. An injury stops a job far longer than a permit does, and a death stops a plant. The fastest repair is the one done properly the first time by people who all go home afterwards. We have never found an exception to that, and we have stopped looking.

Why we do not own three hundred machines

Idle iron is a cost that somebody pays. We decided it would not be our clients.

4 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. What a machine costs when it is standing
  2. What an owner knows
  3. What we add
  4. The objections
  5. The same idea, three more times
  6. What we will own
Field notes
  • Field notes overview

Essays

  • What salt does to concrete
  • The arithmetic of a cold kiln
  • Why we do not own three hundred machines
  • Basalt
  • Night shift in lion country
  • After the storm
  • How to read a shutdown
  • The first bus of the morning
  • The weighbridge
  • One number

Reference

  • Glossary
  • Pocket checklists

People who visit us sometimes ask to see the yard. They have read that we command more than three hundred machines, and they expect a field of yellow steel stretching to the horizon.

There is no such field. The machines are scattered through the villages of this coast, parked beside the houses of the people who own them. This is not an embarrassment. It is the design.

What a machine costs when it is standing

A heavy excavator is an expensive thing, usually bought on a loan. The instalment falls due every month whether the machine has worked or not. So does the insurance. So does the wage of an operator who must be kept, because a good one cannot be found in a week.

A machine that works twenty days in a month earns its keep. A machine that works eight does not, and the difference has to come from somewhere.

In a contracting firm that owns its fleet, it comes from the rates. The cost of the idle days is spread over the working ones. Every client pays a little for machines that were standing in the yard on someone else’s quiet week.

There is a second and subtler cost. A firm with idle machines is under pressure to find them work. It takes jobs it should decline. It sends a 30-tonne excavator to do what a 20-tonne machine would do better, because the 30 is the one standing. It keeps old machines running past their time because they are paid for. The fleet begins to choose the work, when the work ought to choose the fleet.

What an owner knows

Now consider the man who owns one excavator, or three.

He bought the machine with his own money and his family’s. He knows the hour-meter reading without looking. He can hear a pump beginning to fail a week before it does. His operator is his nephew, or himself. When the machine is not earning, he is the one lying awake, so he is on the telephone finding it work, with us, with a quarry, with a road contractor, with whoever has need of it.

His machine is not idle on our quiet weeks. It is working for someone else. So we do not pay for its idleness, and neither do you.

And it is looked after as no fleet machine ever is. A hired operator on a company excavator will run it with a leaking seal until it stops. An owner will not.

What we add

A hundred owners with good machines are not yet a contractor. They cannot sign a contract for a foundation, or answer to a plant’s safety officer, or field twelve machines of the right classes on the same morning.

That is our part. We know who owns what, in what condition, and how far away. We have tried each machine and each operator on real work. We set one standard for all of them. We do the planning, the supervision and the answering. And we pay on the day we said we would, which is why our calls are answered before anyone else’s.

The objections

We have heard them all, and they deserve straight answers.

You do not control the machines. We control something better: the choice. If a machine arrives in poor condition it is sent back and another is called. A firm that owns its fleet has to use what it has.

What if they are all busy when I need them? With more than three hundred in the network, and owners who put our calls first, there is depth to spare. The whole point of depth is that no single machine matters.

An owner-operator will not follow plant rules. An owner-operator who does not follow them is no longer in the network. They know this. See The standard.

It must cost more, with a margin on top. It need not, because nobody in the chain is carrying idle iron.

The same idea, three more times

Once we had seen it work for machines, we saw the same shape everywhere.

A payroll of six hundred, carried through the lean months, is idle iron of another kind. So we built a register.

Twenty tippers bought on loans and waiting for a contract are idle iron. So we built transport partnerships.

A fleet of buses parked from nine to five is idle iron. So is a staff car that waits all week for one airport run.

In each case there were people on this coast who already owned the thing, cared for it better than we could, and wanted steady work for it. In each case what was missing was someone to bind them to a standard and stand in front of the client.

What we will own

We are not opposed to owning things. We are planning a ready-mix plant and a fabrication yard, because concrete and steel are the two materials every schedule waits on, and because there the gain in control is worth the cost.

The test is always the same. Does owning this make the client’s job faster, safer or better? If so, we buy it. If it only makes our yard more impressive to visitors, we do not.

So there is no field of yellow steel. But ask for twelve machines by tomorrow morning, and count what arrives.

Basalt

What ten years of digging the hardest rock in Gujarat have taught us.

5 min read

NBhakodar limestone pits
On this page
  1. What it is like
  2. How it is broken
  3. Dykes
  4. What the rock has taught us
  5. A kind of affection
Field notes
  • Field notes overview

Essays

  • The arithmetic of a cold kiln
  • Why we do not own three hundred machines
  • Basalt
  • Night shift in lion country
  • After the storm
  • How to read a shutdown
  • The first bus of the morning
  • The weighbridge
  • One number

Reference

  • Glossary
  • Pocket checklists

Sixty-five million years ago, give or take, the ground under western India opened and lava came out. It did not come as a volcano comes, from a cone, with ash and thunder. It came from long cracks, as a flood, and spread across the land in sheets. Then it stopped, and cooled, and after a time it came again and laid another sheet on the first.

This went on for longer than the mind can comfortably hold. When it ended, a pile of black rock two kilometres deep in places lay over half a million square kilometres. Geologists call it the Deccan Traps, from an old Swedish word for stairs, because the weathered edges of the flows stand in steps across the landscape.

The southern edge of that pile runs under Amreli district. We have been making holes in it since 2015.

What it is like

Basalt is dense, dark and fine-grained. Strike it with a hammer and it rings. A cubic metre weighs getting on for three tonnes, a good deal more than the limestone that lies above it.

It is not one solid mass, and this is the first thing a digger learns. Each flow cooled from its top and its bottom, shrank, and cracked into blocks and columns. Between one flow and the next there is often a softer band: the weathered top of the older flow, sometimes a red layer of ancient soil baked by the lava that buried it. Near the surface the rock has rotted to a gravelly earth that every contractor in western India knows as moorum.

So a pit in basalt goes down through moorum, then through weathered rock that a bucket can rip, then through blocky rock that needs a breaker, then perhaps through a soft band, then into rock harder than anything above it.

No borehole log tells you this as well as the first day’s digging.

How it is broken

A hydraulic breaker is a steel chisel as thick as a man’s leg, driven by a piston many times a second. It does not cut the rock. It finds the rock’s own cracks and opens them.

A good operator knows this, and never puts the tool in the middle of a sound block and leans on it. That only heats the chisel and shakes the machine. He looks for the joint, sets the point beside it, at a slight angle toward the free face, and gives the rock somewhere to go. Three seconds, and if nothing has moved, he shifts. The rock comes away in pieces the size of a suitcase.

A poor operator makes noise and dust all day and has a small pile to show for it.

The machine matters as much as the man. A breaker is only as good as the carrier behind it. On a 20-tonne excavator a heavy breaker bounces. On a 50-tonne machine it bites. This is the whole reason our network holds the 50-tonne class. In this rock, anything lighter is not slower. It is merely busy.

Dykes

After the floods of lava had ended, the crust cracked again, and fresh molten rock rose into the cracks and froze there. These are dykes: walls of dolerite or pale rhyolite, a metre thick or twenty, standing more or less upright in the older basalt and running for kilometres.

South of Amreli there are many. A dyke is harder than the rock around it, because it cooled slowly, underground. At the surface it often stands up as a low straight ridge, and anyone who knows the country can see where one will cross a road.

Underground you meet it without warning. A trench that was advancing ten metres a shift advances two. There is nothing to be done except to tell the client the same day, bring the second breaker, and be patient.

What the rock has taught us

Send the right machine first. A day spent proving that the small one cannot do it is a day lost and a machine damaged.

Dig a little before you price a lot. A trial pit costs almost nothing. It is the cheapest insurance in construction.

Record the rock as you meet it. Soil and rock are paid differently, and memory is a poor witness. We take levels jointly with the client’s engineer at the top of rock and photograph the faces.

Leave the last hand’s breadth. A breaker does not stop where the drawing says. Rock taken below the line must be made up in concrete at our cost, so the final trim is done slowly.

Mind what stands nearby. A breaker shakes the ground. Beside a running machine or an old wall, the position of the tool and the size of the hammer are chosen with that in mind.

Respect the edge. A rock pit has vertical sides and a hard floor. People and machines stay back from it, it is fenced before dark, and nobody climbs out of it except by a ladder.

A kind of affection

Basalt is a hard master, and after ten years we find that we are fond of it.

A foundation cut into sound basalt will not settle in a thousand years. The rock that breaks our chisels carries the crushers and mills of this coast without complaint. And there is a satisfaction, known to anyone who has done it, in standing at the bottom of a clean square pit cut eight metres into black stone, with the breaker silent at last, and the engineer’s level reading true.

The rock does not negotiate. But it keeps its side of the bargain.

Night shift in lion country

What shares the dark with a tipper on the Pipavav road, and how we drive because of it.

5 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. What the night changes
  2. The road
  3. The other traffic
  4. Why we do not resent it
  5. Morning
Field notes
  • Field notes overview

Essays

  • What salt does to concrete
  • The arithmetic of a cold kiln
  • Why we do not own three hundred machines
  • Basalt
  • Night shift in lion country
  • After the storm
  • How to read a shutdown
  • The first bus of the morning
  • The weighbridge
  • One number

Reference

  • Glossary
  • Pocket checklists

At ten at night the B shift comes out and the C shift goes in. The buses turn round at the gate. For twenty minutes the road is busy, and then it empties, and the night belongs to the people who work it.

What the night changes

A plant does not sleep. The kiln turns at the same speed at three in the morning as at three in the afternoon. But everything around it is altered.

Sound carries. The hum of the mill, which nobody notices by day, fills the whole sky. A dropped spanner is heard across the yard.

Light becomes a thing you have or do not have. Under the floodlights it is brighter than a cloudy noon. One step outside them it is black, and the eye, which has adjusted to the glare, sees nothing at all. Most of the mistakes of the night happen at that edge.

And the body argues. Between two and four it wants to be asleep, whatever it has been told. Attention narrows. A man will look straight at a hazard and not register it.

So the night shift has rules of its own. Work fronts are lit before work starts, not during. Nobody works alone. The supervisor walks more often, and talks to people, because a man who answers slowly is a man who should sit down for ten minutes. Heavy lifts and first entries into vessels are kept for the day wherever the job allows. Tea comes at one.

The road

Out on the road a tipper is carrying aggregate to a night pour.

The driver has done this run a thousand times. The highway is nearly empty. It would be easy to make up time.

He does not, and the reason is standing somewhere ahead of him in the scrub.

This coast belongs to the Asiatic lion, and the lion keeps different hours from ours. By day it lies up in the thorn. At dusk it rises and walks, and it walks where walking is easy, which very often means along a road. In the cool of the night the tarmac holds the day’s warmth, and a pride will lie on it as cattle do.

A tipper’s headlights reach perhaps a hundred metres. Loaded, at speed, it needs most of that to stop. A lion the colour of dry grass, lying on a road the colour of dust, does not show at a hundred metres. What shows first is the eyes: two pale coins, low down, then four, then more.

So our drivers come down this road at night at a speed from which they can stop inside their own lights. When the eyes appear, they stop, well back. They dip the beam. They do not sound the horn. They do not get down. They wait.

It may be two minutes. It may be twenty. A lioness will stand in the road and look at the lorry as though considering whether to buy it. Cubs will sit down and scratch. There is nothing whatever to be done about it, and after the first time a driver stops trying to think of something. He switches off the engine and listens to it tick.

Then they go, without hurry, into the scrub on the other side. He counts to thirty, in case of a straggler, and drives on.

The other traffic

The lion is the grandest thing on the road at night, but not the most dangerous.

That is the blue bull, the nilgai, an antelope the size of a horse, which comes out of a field at a gallop and crosses without looking. Then there are cattle, which sleep on the warm tarmac and do not move for anything. Dogs. A tractor with no lights and a trolley of fodder. A man walking home in dark clothes.

Every one of these is an argument for the same rule. Slower, at night, than seems necessary.

Why we do not resent it

A contractor from the city, told that his trucks must crawl because a lion may be in the road, hears a cost. Twenty minutes on a trip. A late mixer.

We hear it differently. We were born on this coast, and so were our parents, and the savaj was here before any of us. There are fewer than a thousand of them in the world, and all of the wild ones live in Gujarat. That a pride should choose to raise its cubs in the scrub between a cement works and a container port, and that drivers of forty-tonne lorries should stop and wait for them, seems to us to say something rather fine about the place, and we would not change it for a faster road.

Besides, a driver who has learned to stop for a lion has learned to stop. He will stop for a child, and for a cyclist, and for a tired man walking home.

Morning

Towards five the sky over the sea turns grey, then pink. The tower lights look weaker. Somewhere a peacock starts up.

The pour is finished. The last tipper comes back along the road, empty, with its window down. In the half light the driver can see the fields now, and the dark line of the hills, and on one of the hills, quite still, the shape of something large, lying with its head up, watching the day arrive.

He lifts one hand from the wheel. It is not exactly a wave.

Then the A shift buses come over the rise with their headlights on, and the night is done.

This is a picture of a night, put together from many. The rules in it are real. See Lion country.

On the night of 17 May 2021 a cyclone crossed this coast. What it took, and what every builder here learned from it.

The Arabian Sea is a quieter ocean than the Bay of Bengal, and for most of living memory this coast thought of cyclones as something that happened to Odisha. There had been storms. There had not been one like this.

The night

Tauktae formed off Kerala in the middle of May and came north along the whole west coast of India, gathering strength as it came. By the time it reached the latitude of Diu it was the strongest storm to threaten Gujarat in more than twenty years.

It came ashore on the night of 17 May 2021, a little east of Diu, and travelled north-east. Jafrabad and Rajula lay directly under it.

People who were here remember the sound first. Then the dark, when the power went, and the knowledge that it would not be coming back that night or for many nights. Roofs lifted. Trees that had stood for sixty years lay across every road. Electricity poles went down by the thousand, and with them the telephone towers, so that for days nobody could find out what had happened to anybody.

In the morning the coast was a different place.

What it took

Pipavav Port stood idle for the better part of two weeks. A cement jetty was damaged, and the roads that led to it were washed away. Fishing boats at Jafrabad were smashed at their moorings. Salt pans vanished under the surge. Across Amreli district mango and coconut orchards, the work of a generation, were flattened in an hour.

Power did not return to some villages for weeks.

The plants themselves, built of heavy concrete and steel, mostly stood. It was everything around them that failed: the lines that fed them, the roads that served them, the sheeting on their sheds, and the homes of the people who ran them.

How the coast was put back

It was put back by the people who live on it.

Nobody waited to be asked. Whoever had an excavator started it and began clearing the road outside his own village. Whoever had a tractor dragged trees. Tipper owners carried away what the excavators piled. Crane owners lifted poles for the electricity crews. Within days there were machines working on roads all over the taluka, many of them simply because their owners lived there.

Help came from outside, and it was needed and welcome. But the first week belonged to machines that were already here, because a machine two districts away is no use on a road that is blocked.

We draw a lesson from that, and it is the same one this whole site is about.

What builders learned

Every contractor on this coast builds a little differently since that night.

Anything light is a missile. Roofing sheets, scaffold boards, cladding, signboards. In a cyclone they travel hundreds of metres. They are now fixed as though the wind were coming, and when a warning is issued, whatever is loose is brought down or tied.

A crane is a sail. Booms are lowered at the first warning. A crawler crane left standing with its boom up is a danger to everything within its length.

Water goes where it went before. The surge and the rain found every old creek bed and low place, including the ones that had been built over. Drainage is no longer the last item on anyone’s drawing.

Temporary works are still works. Site offices, stores and labour camps were the first things to go. People in temporary accommodation are now moved into solid buildings before a storm arrives, not during it.

Power will be gone. A site that cannot pump out its own excavations without the grid will have ponds for a fortnight. A plant that cannot run its own essentials will have worse.

Stock matters. For a week nothing could be bought, because nothing could be delivered. Diesel, drinking water, tarpaulins, rope.

Nothing is energised until it has been looked at. After the wind, the danger is the fallen wire that is not dead and the structure that looks sound and is not.

What the plants learned

Many a contingency plan had assumed that help would arrive. That week, the roads being what they were, help could only come from inside the circle.

The contractors who mattered were the ones who could walk to the gate.

The calendar now

The sea gives two windows for cyclones, before the monsoon and after it. In those weeks we watch the bulletins, as everyone here now does, and we have a list of what is done when a warning is raised. It is on the page Heat and monsoon.

Most warnings come to nothing. The storm turns towards Oman, or weakens, or crosses the coast somewhere else. Crews grumble at lowering booms for a wind that never comes.

Then they remember May 2021, and they lower the boom.

This note describes what the storm did to the region, from public record and common memory, and what builders here learned from it. It is not an account of any particular firm’s part in the recovery.

How to read a shutdown

Three clocks, one chain, and the signs that tell you by the fourth day whether the plant will light up on time.

4 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. Three clocks
  2. One chain
  3. The surprise
  4. Signs of a shutdown going well
  5. Signs of one going badly
  6. What it comes to
Field notes
  • Field notes overview

Essays

  • What salt does to concrete
  • The arithmetic of a cold kiln
  • Why we do not own three hundred machines
  • Basalt
  • Night shift in lion country
  • After the storm
  • How to read a shutdown
  • The first bus of the morning
  • The weighbridge
  • One number

Reference

  • Glossary
  • Pocket checklists

From outside, a shutdown looks like chaos: several hundred people, a dozen cranes, scaffolding everywhere, three shifts and no sleep. From inside, a good one is as orderly as a railway timetable. The difference between a good one and a bad one can be read quite early, if you know where to look.

Three clocks

A kiln shutdown runs on three clocks, and only one of them belongs to the contractor.

The first is cooling. A kiln that was at fourteen hundred degrees yesterday cannot be entered today. It has to cool, and it cannot be hurried much without damaging the brick that is to be kept. Nobody can shorten this clock. A wise planner fills it with every job that does not need the kiln to be cold.

The second is the work.

The third is heating. New refractory must be dried and brought up to temperature by a schedule. It takes as long as it takes.

The plant has promised its head office a date for clinker. Subtract the heating clock from that date, and the cooling clock from the start, and what is left in the middle is all the time there is. It is always less than anyone would like.

One chain

Inside that window there may be three hundred jobs. Most of them do not matter to the date.

That sounds careless, and it is the most useful thing a shutdown planner can understand. Three hundred jobs, done by different crews in different places, mostly do not depend on each other. If the painters on the cooler stack lose a day, the plant will still light up on time.

But somewhere in the list there is a chain: this job cannot start until that one finishes, which cannot start until another has. Add up the chain and it comes to exactly the length of the window. That is the critical path, and a day lost anywhere on it is a day lost at the end.

In a kiln shutdown the chain usually runs through the kiln itself. Cool. Enter. Strip the old brick. Inspect the shell. Repair what the inspection finds. Lay the new brick. Close. Heat.

Everything else is a side road. The art is to know, every morning, which jobs are on the chain, and to feed them first: the first crane, the best crew, the supervisor who does not need telling.

The surprise

Then the kiln is opened, and something is found.

It always is. A shell plate thinner than it should be. A crack in a tyre. A cyclone whose inner tube has burned half away. Nobody could have known, because nobody could look until now.

Found work is what breaks shutdowns, and whether it does depends on what was decided beforehand. If every person and every hour was already committed, the found job can only be done by taking people off something else, and the whole plan begins to slide. If a reserve was held, a crew with nothing in particular to do and a few days of float, the found job is absorbed and the date holds.

Holding a reserve looks like waste for the first three days. On the fourth it looks like genius.

Signs of a shutdown going well

You can walk on to a site and know within ten minutes.

It is clean. Debris is being carried away as fast as it is made. Walkways are clear. A dirty shutdown is a slow one, because people cannot move.

The meeting is short. Fifteen minutes, standing. Each job: on plan, or not, and what is being done. Nobody is surprised by anything said.

The night shift is working. Not waiting for a permit, a crane or an answer. Shutdowns are won at night, when no managers are watching.

Material is at the work front. Not in a store at the other end of the plant.

The supervisors know their numbers. Ask one how many rings of brick are down, and the answer comes at once.

People are rested. Twelve days of sixteen-hour shifts produce mistakes, and mistakes on a shutdown hurt people.

Signs of one going badly

Jobs are starting and not finishing. Crews are moved from one fire to the next. Half-done work everywhere.

The same item is “tomorrow” three days running.

Crane wars. Two supervisors arguing at the hook about whose lift is next. That argument should have been settled on paper a month ago.

The permit office has a queue.

The scope is still growing on day five, and nobody has said which of the new jobs will not be done.

The contractor’s manager is on the telephone to the plant manager. Whatever they are saying, it means the plan has left the site and gone upstairs.

What it comes to

A shutdown is decided in the six weeks before it starts. By the time the kiln goes cold, the crews are booked or they are not, the steel is cut or it is not, the scaffold is up or it is not. What happens afterwards is mostly the playing out of what was prepared.

That is why we ask to walk the scope six weeks ahead, and why we are tiresome about it. We would rather be tiresome in September than sorry in November.

The first bus of the morning

A plant runs on wheels that nobody notices until the morning they fail to appear.

4 min read

NRajula
On this page
  1. The route
  2. What rides on it
  3. The driver
  4. The spare
  5. The return
Field notes
  • Field notes overview

Essays

  • What salt does to concrete
  • The arithmetic of a cold kiln
  • Why we do not own three hundred machines
  • Basalt
  • Night shift in lion country
  • After the storm
  • How to read a shutdown
  • The first bus of the morning
  • The weighbridge
  • One number

Reference

  • Glossary
  • Pocket checklists

The first bus leaves at ten minutes to five.

Its driver has been up since four. He has walked round the vehicle with a torch, as he does every morning: tyres, lights, the emergency door. He has started the engine and let it run while he drinks his tea standing up. Now he pulls out of the yard into a town that is still dark, with one light on in the bakery and a dog asleep in the middle of the road.

The route

He makes nine stops. He could drive the route blindfold, and in the monsoon, before dawn, it sometimes feels as though he does.

At each stop there are people waiting who have judged the time to the minute. They know that this bus comes at eight past five, not at five past and not at ten past, so they have left their houses at exactly the moment that brings them to the corner with their tea finished. A bus that runs to the minute gives every one of its passengers ten more minutes of sleep. A bus that is sometimes early and sometimes late takes those minutes back, from fifty people, every day.

Nobody on the bus thinks about this. That is the proof that it is working.

What rides on it

By half past five there are fifty people aboard. Between them they will run a kiln, two mills, a packing plant and a power station for the next eight hours.

At six the shift changes. Not at five past. The burner who has been watching the flame since ten the night before stands up from his chair when his relief walks in, and not until. If the relief is on a bus that has broken down eleven kilometres away, the night man stays. He has been awake for most of twenty hours, and he is in charge of a tube of fire sixty metres long.

That is what a late bus costs. Not inconvenience. A tired man at the controls.

And it is why the people who run plants, who have enormous matters to think about, will ring a contractor personally about a bus.

The driver

A plant’s shift bus driver is known to more of its people than the plant manager is. He sees them every day at their least guarded, half awake on the way in and worn out on the way home. He knows who has a new baby by who is asleep before the second stop.

A good one has certain habits. He brakes early and gently, because people are standing to get off. He does not use the horn in the villages at five in the morning. He waits ten seconds for the man running, and only ten. He slows right down on the stretch by the scrub, because twice now he has come round that bend and found the road full of lions.

He never, under any circumstances, looks at his telephone.

We choose our drivers for those habits more than for anything on their licence.

The spare

Buses break down. It is not a disgrace. A fan belt goes, a tyre finds a nail.

What matters is what happens in the next fifteen minutes. On a route we run, the driver rings the coordinator, who is awake because it is his business to be. A spare bus, with a spare driver, is already in a yard a few kilometres away, and it leaves at once. The passengers are twenty minutes late and the shift in-charge has been told why before they arrive.

On a route run by a man with one bus, the passengers stand at the roadside and the night shift stays on.

That spare bus sits idle on most days, and somebody has to carry its cost. Spread over a network of routes, it is a small cost. For an owner with one contract, it is impossible. This is the whole argument for a fleet run as a network, and it fits in a single yard.

The return

At a quarter past two the same bus is at the gate again, taking the A shift home and bringing nobody in, because the B shift came on another.

The people who got on in the dark get off in the glare. The burner is among them. He has made, by his own attention, some sixteen hundred tonnes of clinker since six this morning, and he is thinking about his lunch.

The driver watches him go, checks his mirror, and pulls away.

He will be up again at four.

A picture of a morning, put together from many. The driver stands for the drivers who do this work.

The weighbridge

A steel deck, four load cells and a printer. It is the most honest machine in a plant, and the place where everyone’s honesty is tested.

4 min read

NCement works, Kovaya
On this page
  1. How it works
  2. The old tricks
  3. Why we do not
  4. The other honesty
  5. Reconciliation
  6. The queue
Field notes
  • Field notes overview

Essays

  • What salt does to concrete
  • The arithmetic of a cold kiln
  • Why we do not own three hundred machines
  • Basalt
  • Night shift in lion country
  • After the storm
  • How to read a shutdown
  • The first bus of the morning
  • The weighbridge
  • One number

Reference

  • Glossary
  • Pocket checklists

Everything that enters a cement plant by road, and everything that leaves, crosses a weighbridge. In Gujarati it is the kanto. In Hindi, the kanta. In either language the word also means a thorn, and there is a certain justice in that.

How it works

A lorry drives on to the deck and stops. Beneath the deck, load cells feel its weight and a figure appears on a screen in the cabin. That is the gross weight: lorry, load, fuel and driver.

The lorry goes in, tips its load and comes back empty. It is weighed again. That is the tare.

Gross less tare is the net: what was actually delivered. The printer makes a slip. The slip is money.

ATKAYVA

Weighbridge slip

SPECIMEN
Vehicle
GJ-14 tipper
Material
Aggregate, 20 mm
Gross
28,460 kg
Tare
10,920 kg
Net
17,540 kg
In
06:42
Out
06:58

Nothing could be simpler. And because the slip is money, people have been trying to argue with it for as long as there have been weighbridges.

The old tricks

We set these down because a client is entitled to know what we guard against, and because anyone who works with us should know that we know.

A lorry weighed in with a full fuel tank and two spare wheels, and weighed out with neither. A driver who stays in the cab for the gross and steps out for the tare. A lorry that stops with its front wheels just off the end of the deck. Water in the load. A slip from yesterday presented today. A load weighed, and then not tipped, and weighed in again an hour later at another gate.

And the commonest of all, which needs no trick: a friendly word in the cabin, and a figure typed in by hand.

Each of these is theft. Each has been tried on this coast by somebody.

Why we do not

A contractor who hauls by the tonne is paid by the slip. A few hundred kilograms a load, over thousands of loads, is a great deal of money. We know contractors who regard it as part of the trade.

We do not, and the reason is not only that it is wrong, though it is. The reason is that a client who has once caught a contractor at the weighbridge never again believes a word that contractor says. Every measurement, every hour, every invoice is doubted. We sell trust. It would be a strange economy to spend it on gravel.

So our drivers are told once. The weight is the weight. A driver who is caught adjusting it is finished with us, and so is the transporter who sent him. If a weighbridge clerk suggests an arrangement, the driver reports it. If one of our own people suggests it, the leadership want to know.

The other honesty

There is a second way to cheat a weighbridge, and it is the opposite of the first: to put too much on.

A tipper built to carry seventeen tonnes will hold twenty-five if you heap it. Paid by the tonne, that is three trips’ money for two trips’ diesel. The lorry’s springs, brakes and tyres pay for it. So does the road. So, when the brakes are asked to stop a load they were never built for, does whoever is in front.

Overloading is illegal, and the weighbridge is where it shows. A plant that turns back an overloaded lorry at the gate is doing the transporter a favour he will not thank it for.

We load to the registered weight. See the slip above: 28,460 kilograms gross, for a three-axle tipper whose legal limit is 28,500.

Reconciliation

At the end of each month there are two columns of figures. Ours, from the slips our drivers bring back. The plant’s, from its own system.

They should agree. Usually they do. When they do not, we do not send the bill and argue afterwards. We sit down with the plant’s stores people and go through the slips until the difference is found. It is nearly always a missed entry or a transposed digit, and it takes an hour.

That hour is the cheapest thing we do all month. A bill that matches the client’s own records is paid without discussion. A bill that does not is paid late, after a fight, and remembered.

The queue

One more thing about the weighbridge, which has nothing to do with honesty.

It is a bottleneck. Every lorry must cross it twice, and at shift change, or when a rake has come in, the queue can stretch out of the gate and down the road.

A transporter who knows a plant knows its weighbridge: when it is busy, when the clerk goes for tea, which deck takes trailers. Our drivers time their runs round it. Over a month, that knowledge is worth several loads a day, and it appears on nobody’s rate card.

The most honest machine in the plant, and the most patient. It has heard every story. It prints the same slip regardless.

One number

Why a firm that commands three hundred machines and six hundred people still has one telephone, and still answers it.

3 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. Two in the morning
  2. The first telephone
  3. What grew, and what did not
  4. What one number promises
  5. The test
Field notes
  • Field notes overview

Essays

  • What salt does to concrete
  • The arithmetic of a cold kiln
  • Why we do not own three hundred machines
  • Basalt
  • Night shift in lion country
  • After the storm
  • How to read a shutdown
  • The first bus of the morning
  • The weighbridge
  • One number

Reference

  • Glossary
  • Pocket checklists

There is a telephone number at the foot of every page on this site. It is the same one each time.

Large firms do not work this way. A large firm has a number for sales and another for service, a helpline that plays music, and an out-of-hours message that gives a third number, which rings in another city. All of this is done in the name of efficiency, and from the firm’s side perhaps it is.

From the other side it looks different.

Two in the morning

Consider who is ringing.

An engineer, on nights. Something has failed that he cannot fix with the people he has. He has rung his own manager, who has said, get somebody. He is standing in a control room with a kiln running down and a list of contractors on the wall.

He does not want a menu. He does not want to explain to a stranger in a call centre what a preheater is. He wants to hear a voice that says: which plant, which gate, where inside. He wants to know within thirty seconds that somebody who understands is already putting on his boots.

Every contractor on that wall claims to offer this. He will find out which of them does by dialling.

The first telephone

In 2015 there was no question of how the telephone should be answered, because there was one founder and one telephone.

It rang at all hours. It was answered at all hours, because an unanswered call was a job that went to someone else, and there were not enough jobs that any could be spared. The plants learned the number. More to the point, they learned that it worked.

That is the whole origin of what we now call emergency response. Nobody designed it. A telephone was answered when others were not, and a reputation grew up round the fact.

What grew, and what did not

The firm is larger now. There are project managers and supervisors, a register of six hundred, a network of three hundred machines. Any sensible adviser would say that the founder of such a firm should not be taking calls at two in the morning.

We have not taken the advice, for a reason we think is sound.

The moment a client is put through to a department, the firm has become the kind of firm that has departments. The engineer in the control room can hear the difference in the first three seconds. He has stopped speaking to someone who can decide and begun speaking to someone who can take a message.

So there is still one number. It is answered by a person who can set the response in motion without asking anyone’s leave. Behind that person stand the project managers, each of whom can be reached by the client they look after, at any hour. But the number on the wall has not changed, and neither has what happens when it rings.

What one number promises

It is a small thing, and it stands for everything else.

One number means one firm to call, whatever is wrong: a crack, a jam, a missing bus, a machine that will not start. The caller does not have to diagnose the problem first in order to know whom to ring.

One number means one firm to blame. The machine came from an owner in one village, the crew from a contractor in another, the lorry from a third. None of that is the caller’s concern. He rang us.

And one number means that the firm cannot hide. A company with a switchboard can be unavailable. A person with a telephone in a pocket either answers it or does not.

The test

We have said a good deal on this site about doctrine, method and proximity. All of it can be checked in a simpler way.

Ring the number. Do it at an inconvenient hour, if you like.

Somebody will answer. They will ask you which plant, and which gate.

The number

One number, answered at any hour. It is on the Contact page.

Contact

Glossary of the corridor

The words you will hear at a plant gate on this coast, in English, in Gujarati and in the language of the trade. If you are new to cement, to construction or to Saurashtra, start here.

6 min read

NKovaya
Field notes
  • Field notes overview

Essays

  • What salt does to concrete
  • The arithmetic of a cold kiln
  • Why we do not own three hundred machines
  • Basalt
  • Night shift in lion country
  • After the storm
  • How to read a shutdown
  • The first bus of the morning
  • The weighbridge
  • One number

Reference

  • Glossary
  • Pocket checklists
A, B and C shift
The three eight-hour shifts most plants here work: 06:00 to 14:00, 14:00 to 22:00 and 22:00 to 06:00. The general shift, or G shift, keeps office hours.
Aggregate
Crushed stone and sand, the bulk of concrete. Sold by size: 10 mm, 20 mm, 40 mm.
Alignment
Setting a machine so that its shafts and surfaces are exactly where the maker’s drawing says, relative to each other and to the foundation.
Annual rate contract
An agreement that fixes rates for a year, so that jobs can be called off without a fresh tender each time. Often shortened to ARC.
Bar bender
The tradesman who cuts, bends and fixes reinforcement steel.
Basalt
The hard, dark volcanic rock that underlies this district. See Basalt.
Batching plant
Where cement, aggregate, water and admixtures are weighed and mixed into concrete.
Bill of quantities
The list of items in a job, each with a quantity and a rate. Usually called the BOQ.
Blended cement
Cement in which part of the clinker is replaced by fly ash or slag. Denser, slower to harden and better against salt.
Brass
A measure of volume used across Gujarat and Maharashtra for sand, stone and earth. One brass is 100 cubic feet, or about 2.83 cubic metres.
Breaker
A hydraulic hammer mounted on an excavator, for breaking rock and concrete.
Bulker
A sealed road tanker for cement or fly ash, emptied by compressed air.
Challan
A delivery or despatch note that travels with goods. Also the receipt for a statutory payment.
Chloride
The part of sea salt that attacks reinforcement. See What salt does to concrete.
Clinker
The hard grey nodules that come out of a kiln. Ground with gypsum, it becomes cement.
Cold joint
A plane of weakness where fresh concrete was placed against concrete that had already begun to set.
Confined space
A vessel, silo, pit or duct with limited entry and a risk of bad air. Entered only under permit.
Cover
The thickness of concrete between a reinforcing bar and the surface. The bar’s protection against rust.
Cube
A 150 mm test cube of concrete, cast at the pour and crushed at 7 and 28 days to prove strength.
Curing
Keeping new concrete wet so that it can finish hardening.
Cyclone
Two meanings on this coast. A storm from the sea. And a conical vessel in a preheater tower that separates hot meal from gas.
Daily progress report
The one page a client receives each day. Often shortened to DPR.
Dry film thickness
The thickness of a coat of paint once dry, measured with a gauge. Often shortened to DFT.
Dry lean concrete
A stiff, rolled concrete layer under a road slab. Often shortened to DLC.
Dyke
A wall of hard rock that rose molten into a crack in older rock. Also, a containment wall round a tank.
E-way bill
The electronic document that must accompany goods moved by road under the GST law.
ESI
Employees’ State Insurance. Medical and cash benefits for insured workers and their families.
Fire watch
A person who does nothing during hot work except watch for fire, extinguisher in hand.
Fly ash
Fine ash from coal-fired power stations. Blended into cement and concrete.
Found work
Repair that is discovered only when a plant is opened during a shutdown.
Gate pass
Permission for a person, vehicle or material to enter or leave a plant.
Gross, tare and net
A loaded vehicle’s weight, its empty weight, and the difference. See The weighbridge.
Grouting
Filling the gap between a machine’s base and its foundation with a flowing, non-shrinking mortar.
GSTIN
Goods and Services Tax Identification Number. It is printed on every tax invoice.
Guniting
Spraying concrete at high velocity on to a surface. Also called shotcrete.
Hot work
Any work that makes sparks or flame: welding, cutting, grinding.
Hydra
The plant name for a pick-and-carry mobile crane.
Isolation
Cutting a machine off from every source of energy, locking the switch, tagging it and trying the start button, before anyone touches it. Also called lock-out and tag-out.
Kanto, kanta
The weighbridge, in Gujarati and in Hindi.
Kiln
The rotating, brick-lined steel tube in which raw meal is burned into clinker at about 1,450 °C.
Light-up
The moment a kiln is fired again after a shutdown.
Lost-time incident
An injury that keeps a person away from work. Often shortened to LTI.
Low-loader
A trailer with a low deck for carrying heavy machines.
Mass concrete
A pour large enough that its own heat must be managed.
Matka
A clay pot that cools drinking water by evaporation.
Millwright
A fitter who specialises in installing and aligning machinery.
Miliolite
The limestone of this coast, made of the shells of small sea creatures.
Moorum
Gravelly earth formed where basalt has weathered. Used for filling and for village roads.
Mukadam
A crew leader or labour foreman.
NABL
The National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories. A laboratory it has accredited can be relied on.
OEM
Original equipment manufacturer. The maker of a machine.
Over-dimensional cargo
A load longer, wider, higher or heavier than the ordinary limits. Often shortened to ODC.
PAN
Permanent Account Number, issued by the Income Tax Department.
Pavement quality concrete
The high-strength concrete of a road slab. Often shortened to PQC.
Permit to work
The plant’s written authority to do a particular job in a particular place at a particular time. Often shortened to PTW.
PF
Provident fund. A retirement saving to which worker and employer both contribute.
Plain cement concrete
Concrete without reinforcement, as in a blinding layer. Often shortened to PCC.
Preheater
The tower in which raw meal is heated by kiln gas on its way to the kiln.
Principal employer
The owner of a plant, who in law has duties towards the workers a contractor brings in.
Raw meal
Limestone and correctives, ground to powder and ready for the kiln.
Ready-mix concrete
Concrete batched at a plant and delivered in transit mixers. Often shortened to RMC.
Refractory
Heat-resisting brick or castable that lines kilns, coolers and cyclones.
Request for inspection
A request to the client’s engineer to inspect a stage of work before it is covered. Often shortened to RFI.
Rigger
The tradesman who slings loads and signals to the crane.
Savaj
The lion, in the Kathiawadi speech of this coast.
Shutdown
A planned stoppage of a plant for maintenance. Also called a turnaround.
Slump
A quick site test of how workable fresh concrete is.
Snag
A small defect or unfinished item found at inspection.
Tiffin
A stack of steel boxes carrying a worker’s lunch from home.
TMT bar
Thermo-mechanically treated reinforcing bar. The ribbed steel in modern concrete.
Toolbox talk
A short safety briefing at the work front before each shift.
Tremie
A pipe through which concrete is placed under water or drilling fluid, from the bottom up.
Tremix
A common name for vacuum-dewatered flooring, after a maker of the equipment.
UAN
Universal Account Number. A worker’s provident fund number, which stays the same from one employer to the next.
Vacuum-dewatered flooring
A concrete floor from which surplus water is sucked out before finishing. Often shortened to VDF.
Weighbridge
A platform scale for lorries. See The weighbridge.
Zero-interference
Our way of working. The client assigns the task and we absorb the complexity. See The Zero-Interference Doctrine.
